fields.h1: Why Would a Good God Allow Suffering?
fields.meta_title: Why Would a Good God Allow Suffering?
fields.description: If God is good and all-powerful, why is there so much pain? An honest look at the hardest question — free will, the cross, Romans 8:28, and a world made right.
fields.body_html:
If God is good and God is all-powerful, why is the world so full of pain? This is the oldest and hardest honest question anyone can ask, and if you are asking it because something has actually happened to you — a death, an illness, an injustice, a home coming apart — then you deserve more than a slogan. The short answer is not that suffering does not matter, or that it is secretly nice, but that the God of the Bible neither causes evil for fun nor stands back from it: he entered it himself, he is working through it toward good, and he has promised to end it. That is worth taking slowly.

So let us take it slowly, without flinching and without pretending it does not hurt.

This really is the hardest question — and the Bible knows it

Start here: your question is not a sign that your faith is weak, and it is not new. The Bible itself asks it, loudly, again and again. A whole book — Job — is given over to a good man who loses his children, his health, and his wealth in a single stretch of catastrophe and then spends thirty-some chapters demanding an answer from God. The Psalms are full of the same raw cry. “How long, O Lord? Will you forget me forever?” one of them begins (Psalm 13:1), and it is not a rebuke that made it into Scripture — it is a prayer God chose to keep.

Even Jesus, dying, quoted a psalm of abandonment: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46). If the Son of God can say that from the cross, then the question is not off-limits to you. Anyone who answers your pain with a tidy formula — everything happens for a reason, you just have to smile — is not reading the same Bible. The God of Scripture does not ask you to muffle the question. He invites you to bring it to him, and he is not fragile.

So please do not add a second wound to your first by believing that doubting, or grieving, or being angry, puts you outside his reach. It does not. The people in the Bible who wrestled hardest with God — Job, Jeremiah, David, Habakkuk — are not held up as failures. They are held up as people who took God seriously enough to argue with him, and he met every one of them.

A world that can love is a world that can break

Why is there suffering at all? Part of the answer is that God made a world with real freedom in it — creatures who could genuinely love, which means creatures who could genuinely turn away. Love that cannot be refused is not love; it is a machine following its wiring. To make beings capable of loving him and one another, God made beings capable of choosing cruelty, selfishness, and harm. And, from the very beginning, they did.

A great deal of the world’s suffering flows straight out of that: wars, abuse, betrayal, greed, neglect, the thousand ways people wound one another. When someone hurts you, that is not God’s doing; it is a human being misusing the freedom that makes them human. God could prevent all of it only by unmaking the very thing that lets us love at all.

But not all suffering is somebody’s fault, and it is dishonest to pretend otherwise. Earthquakes, cancer, birth defects, the slow failures of a body — these are not the malice of a bully. The Bible’s picture is that the whole created order is out of joint, “groaning” under a brokenness that touches everything (Romans 8:22). We live in a world that is not the way it is supposed to be, and we feel that wrongness precisely because we were made for something better. Your sense that suffering is an outrage, that it should not be, is not an argument against God. It is a clue that you were built for a world without it — a world that has been lost, and that God intends to give back.

God did not stay outside it — he entered it

Here is where the Christian answer parts company with every philosophy that keeps God at a safe distance. Most attempts to explain suffering leave God up in the clouds, unbothered, watching us from a comfortable height. The gospel does the opposite. It says that God came down into the pain himself.

Jesus was, in the words of the prophet, “a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief” (Isaiah 53:3). He was poor, misunderstood, betrayed by a friend, deserted by the rest, falsely accused, tortured, and executed. When his friend Lazarus died, Jesus — who knew he was minutes away from raising him — still stood at the grave and “wept” (John 11:35). God in the flesh cried real tears at a real tomb. He did not think death was no big deal. He hated it, and he wept.

And then, on the cross, he took the full weight of the world’s evil into himself. This is the strange heart of the Christian faith: the answer to suffering is not mainly an explanation, it is a person, and that person has scars. When you cry out, “God, do you even know what this feels like?” — the Christian answer is yes. He knows from the inside. He does not offer comfort from a distance; he offers it from a cross. A God who suffered for you is a God you can trust in your own suffering, even when you cannot yet understand it.

The difference between “why” and “what now”

Notice something about the book of Job. Job spends the whole book demanding to know why — and when God finally answers him, out of the whirlwind, he never actually tells Job why. Instead he takes Job on a tour of the wildness and vastness of creation, essentially asking: Do you trust that I am wise and good, even where you cannot see the whole picture? (Job 38-41). And astonishingly, that is enough for Job. Not a reason — a relationship. Job says, in effect, I had heard of you, but now I have seen you (Job 42:5).

This matters for you. In the middle of real pain, the “why” question often has no answer you could bear to hear anyway — and demanding one can keep you locked in place. The more livable question is usually not why did this happen but what do I do now, and who will walk with me through it. God rarely hands us the reason. He reliably hands us himself. “The Lord is near to the brokenhearted, and saves the crushed in spirit” (Psalm 34:18) — not the fixed, not the strong, but the crushed. He does not wait for you to climb out of the pit. He comes down into it.

So it is completely fair to keep asking why. But do not put your life on hold until the answer arrives. Turn the question, gently, toward the God who is near: What now? Will you help me carry this? Will you stay? Those prayers get answered.

“God works it for good” — what Romans 8:28 actually says

You have probably heard someone quote Romans 8:28 at a funeral: “And we know that for those who love God all things work together for good” (Romans 8:28). Too often it is used as a lid slammed down on grief — so cheer up, this is all for the best. That is a misuse, and it wounds people.

Look at what the verse actually says, and what it does not. It does not say that all things are good. Cancer is not good. Abuse is not good. A child’s death is not good, and the Bible never asks you to call it good. What it says is that God works — actively, patiently — in and through even the worst things, to bring about good he can weave out of them. The evil stays evil; God is simply greater than it, and refuses to let it have the final say.

The clearest picture of this is Joseph, sold into slavery by his own brothers, imprisoned on a lie, forgotten for years. Decades later, with the power to destroy them, he says instead: “You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good” (Genesis 50:20). Notice he does not rewrite history. What his brothers did was evil, and he says so plainly. But God was at work the whole time, in the dark, bending even that betrayal toward the rescue of many lives. That is the promise: not that the wound was secretly a gift, but that God is a master at bringing life out of what was meant for death.

You may not see the good for a long time. Joseph waited more than twenty years. Some of it we will not see this side of eternity. But the promise is not that you will always understand — it is that nothing in your suffering is wasted in the hands of a God who is still writing the story.

A world that will be made right

Christianity does not finally answer suffering with a theory. It answers with a future. The whole story is heading somewhere, and where it is heading is the undoing of every hurt. At the end of the Bible, God shows John a renewed world and makes a promise so specific it is almost unbearable to read when you are grieving: “He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain anymore, for the former things have passed away” (Revelation 21:4).

Every tear — including yours, including the ones you cried alone that nobody saw. Death gone. Mourning gone. The former things passed away. This is not a vague hope that things will feel a bit better someday. It is the claim that a real world is coming, as solid as this one, where the very sources of your pain have been abolished, and God himself does the wiping of the tears.

And the reason a Christian dares to believe it is the empty tomb. Jesus did not just teach about a world made right; he walked out of his own grave as the first piece of it. Because he rose, death is a defeated enemy and, for those who trust him, a doorway rather than a wall. Jesus was honest that this life would be hard — “In the world you will have tribulation,” he said — but he did not stop there: “take heart; I have overcome the world” (John 16:33). The pain is real. So is the promise. And the promise outlasts the pain.

What to do with your pain right now

So where does all this leave you tonight, if you are hurting? Not with a formula, but with a few honest things you can actually do.

  • Tell God the truth, all of it. The Psalms are permission slips for honesty — anger, confusion, even accusation, poured out to the only One strong enough to hold it. “Pour out your heart before him,” Scripture says (Psalm 62:8). You do not have to perform a peace you do not feel. He would rather have your honest anguish than your polite distance.
  • Do not carry it alone. Suffering isolates; that is one of its cruelest tricks. Let trusted people in — a parent, a pastor, a friend, a counselor. God very often does his comforting through other human beings, and reaching for help is strength, not weakness.
  • Hold the two truths together. You can grieve deeply and hope deeply at the same time. Christians are not told they will not grieve, only that they need not grieve “as others do who have no hope” (1 Thessalonians 4:13). Tears and hope can flow together, and often do.

Here is the thing worth walking away with. The Bible never promises that your suffering will make sense to you soon, and it refuses to insult you by calling evil good. What it promises is a God who is not distant from your pain but has scars of his own; who is near to the brokenhearted; who is quietly working even this toward a good you cannot yet see; and who has promised, on the strength of an empty tomb, to wipe every tear away and end all pain forever.

You do not have to have all the answers to bring your broken heart to a God like that. You can come with the questions still burning. Jesus himself invited exactly this: “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28). Not “come once you have it figured out.” Come now, as you are, carrying what you carry. He knows what it weighs. He is near, he understands, and he has promised to carry you all the way home.
